title: Adding and Subtracting Bigger Numbers
bigQuestion: How do hundreds, tens and ones help us add and subtract big numbers?

story.title: The Lemonade Stand
story.kicker: Two days of sales, two cards with numbers and one big question: how many cups in all?
paragraphs: It is a hot weekend in July. Kai and Rosa set up a lemonade stand on the corner. A cup costs 50 cents. Saturday is busy. Cars stop. Neighbors walk over. By dinner they have sold 48 cups. Rosa writes 48 on a card.

Sunday is a little slower. Clouds roll in after lunch. Still, they sell 36 cups. Rosa writes 36 on a second card. Kai looks at the two cards. How many cups did we sell in all? he asks. Rosa starts to count on her fingers. That will take forever.

Then Rosa remembers the button jar. Tens and ones! she says. 48 is 4 tens and 8 ones. 36 is 3 tens and 6 ones. Add the tens: 7 tens. Add the ones: 14 ones. But 14 ones is a ten and 4 more. So that is 8 tens and 4 ones. Eighty-four cups!

Kai checks it another way. 48 plus 30 is 78. Then 78 plus 6 is 84. Same answer. They high-five. Then Kai asks a harder question. We had 100 cups at the start. How many are left? That is a subtraction problem. And it is next.
story.think: Rosa and Kai got 84 two different ways. Why is it smart to check an answer with a second way?

lessons.title: Tens With Tens, Ones With Ones
lessons.mainIdea: To add two-digit numbers, add the tens together and the ones together.
reading: Let's *add* 32 + 45. Break each number apart. 32 is 3 tens and 2 ones. 45 is 4 tens and 5 ones. Add the tens: 3 tens + 4 tens = 7 tens. Add the ones: 2 + 5 = 7. So 32 + 45 = 77.
Picture the rods and cubes. Put 3 rods next to 4 rods. That is 7 rods. Put 2 cubes next to 5 cubes. That is 7 cubes. 7 rods and 7 cubes show 77. The *sum* is 77.
A common mistake is to add a ten to a one. In 32 + 45, do not add 3 + 5. The 3 is tens and the 5 is ones. Tens go with tens. Ones go with ones.

words.d: to put amounts together and find the total
the answer you get when you add

look.title: Rods and Cubes
look.text: Picture 5 rods of ten and 1 cube. That is 51. Now picture 2 rods and 6 cubes. That is 26. Push all the rods together. Push all the cubes together. Count the rods. Count the cubes.
look.prompt: What is 51 + 26? How many rods and cubes do you end with?

check.why: 2 tens + 5 tens = 7 tens. 3 + 4 = 7 ones. So 77.
4 tens + 3 tens = 7 tens. 1 + 6 = 7 ones. So 77.

check.q: In 62 + 15, which two digits are both tens?
check.why: 6 is the tens digit in 62. 1 is the tens digit in 15. Add them to get 7 tens.

lessons.title: Trading Ten Ones for a Ten
lessons.mainIdea: When the ones add up to 10 or more, trade ten ones for one ten.
reading: Add 48 + 36. Ones first: 8 + 6 = 14. That is too many ones. 14 ones is 1 ten and 4 ones. Trade ten of them for a rod. When you trade like this, you *regroup*.
Now count the tens. 4 tens + 3 tens = 7 tens. Add the new ten from the trade. 7 + 1 = 8 tens. So 48 + 36 is 8 tens and 4 ones. That is 84.
The big mistake is to forget the traded ten. Then you get 74 instead of 84. Always ask: did my ones make a ten? If yes, add it to the tens.

words.d: to trade ten ones for one ten, or one ten for ten ones

look.title: Too Many Cubes
look.text: Picture 2 rods and 7 cubes. Now add 1 rod and 5 cubes. Push the cubes together. You have 12 cubes. Ten of them can snap into a new rod. Now count all the rods. Count the cubes left over.
look.prompt: What is 27 + 15? How many rods did you end with after the trade?

check.why: 7 + 8 = 15. Trade for 1 ten and 5 ones. 5 + 2 + 1 = 8 tens. So 85.
9 + 4 = 13. Trade ten ones for a ten. 3 + 4 + 1 = 8 tens. So 83.

check.q: Kai adds 46 + 27 and gets 63. What did he forget?
check.why: 6 + 7 = 13 makes a ten. 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 tens. The answer is 73, not 63.

lessons.title: Adding Three or Four Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: Add several numbers by finding friendly pairs and keeping tens and ones straight.
reading: Add 12 + 25 + 18. Look for a *friendly pair* that makes a ten. 12 + 18 = 30. That is easy. Then 30 + 25 = 55. So 12 + 25 + 18 = 55.
Try four numbers: 21 + 14 + 19 + 26. Pair 21 + 19 = 40. Pair 14 + 26 = 40. Then 40 + 40 = 80. Check it: the ones are 1 + 4 + 9 + 6 = 20. The tens are 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6 tens. 60 + 20 = 80.
You can add in any order. The sum stays the same. Pick the order that makes tens. If nothing pairs up, add the tens, then add the ones, then trade.

words.d: two numbers that are easy to add, like 12 + 18 = 30

look.title: Cups Sold in Four Days
look.cite: Kai and Rosa's lemonade stand, example numbers
look.prompt: How many cups in all four days? Which two numbers make a friendly pair?

check.q: Which pair is a friendly pair that makes tens?
check.why: 25 + 15 = 40. The ones 5 + 5 make a ten with none left over.

lessons.title: Subtracting Tens and Ones
lessons.mainIdea: To subtract, take tens from tens and ones from ones.
reading: Let's *subtract* 68 − 25. Take the tens first. 6 tens − 2 tens = 4 tens. Now the ones. 8 − 5 = 3. So 68 − 25 = 43. The *difference* is 43. Check by adding: 43 + 25 = 68.
Picture 6 rods and 8 cubes. Take away 2 rods. Take away 5 cubes. You have 4 rods and 3 cubes left. That is 43.
A number line helps too. Start at 68. Jump back 20 to 48. Jump back 5 to 43. Big jump for the tens, small jump for the ones.

words.d: to take away part of an amount and find what is left
the answer you get when you subtract

look.title: Cups Left
look.text: Kai and Rosa start Saturday with 89 empty cups. They sell 48 cups. Picture 8 stacks of ten cups and 9 loose cups. Take away 4 stacks. Take away 8 loose cups. How many stacks and loose cups are left?
look.prompt: How many cups are left? Say the tens and the ones.

check.why: 7 tens − 3 tens = 4 tens. 9 − 4 = 5. So 45.
9 tens − 5 tens = 4 tens. The 6 ones stay. So 46.
Add the answer back: 35 + 23 = 58. It matches the start, so the check works.

lessons.title: Trading a Ten for Ten Ones
lessons.mainIdea: When there are not enough ones to subtract, break one ten into ten ones.
reading: Subtract 52 − 17. Look at the ones. 2 − 7 does not work. There are not enough ones. So *trade* one ten for ten ones. Now you have 4 tens and 12 ones.
Now subtract. 12 − 7 = 5. Then 4 tens − 1 ten = 3 tens. So 52 − 17 = 35. Check: 35 + 17 = 52. Yes.
The common mistake is to flip the ones. Some students do 7 − 2 = 5 and 5 − 1 = 4 and get 45. That is wrong. You cannot flip. Trade a ten instead.

words.d: to swap one ten for ten ones so you can subtract

look.title: Breaking a Rod
look.text: Picture 4 rods and 3 cubes. That is 43. You need to take away 8 cubes. There are only 3. Break one rod into 10 cubes. Now you have 3 rods and 13 cubes. Take away 8 cubes. Count what is left.
look.prompt: What is 43 − 8? How many rods and cubes are left?

check.why: Trade: 5 tens and 13 ones. 13 − 8 = 5. 5 − 2 = 3 tens. So 35.
Trade: 7 tens and 10 ones. 10 − 6 = 4. 7 − 4 = 3 tens. So 34.

check.q: In 71 − 25, why do you trade a ten?
check.why: You cannot take 5 ones from 1 one. Trade a ten to get 11 ones. 71 − 25 = 46.

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting to 1,000
lessons.mainIdea: With hundreds, add or subtract hundreds, tens and ones each in their own place.
reading: Add 235 + 142. Draw it. Squares for hundreds, lines for tens, dots for ones. 2 squares + 1 square = 3 hundreds. 3 lines + 4 lines = 7 tens. 5 dots + 2 dots = 7 ones. So 377.
Sometimes you trade into the *hundreds place*. Add 356 + 271. Tens: 5 + 7 = 12 tens. Ten tens make a hundred! Trade. 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 hundreds. 2 tens. 7 ones. So 627.

words.d: the third spot from the right in a number; it counts groups of 100

look.title: Draw It Out
look.text: Draw 3 squares, 2 lines and 4 dots. That shows 324. Now draw 1 square, 5 lines and 3 dots for 153. Count all the squares. Count all the lines. Count all the dots.
look.prompt: What is 324 + 153? What does your drawing show?

check.why: 4 + 3 = 7 hundreds. 1 + 5 = 6 tens. 2 + 6 = 8 ones. So 768.
5 − 2 = 3 hundreds. 8 − 6 = 2 tens. 9 − 4 = 5 ones. So 325.
4 tens + 8 tens = 12 tens. That is 1 hundred and 2 tens. 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 hundreds. So 620.

lessons.title: Mental Math with 10s and 100s
lessons.mainIdea: You can add or subtract 10 or 100 in your head by changing one digit.
reading: Rosa sold 48 cups. Then 10 more. She uses *mental math*. She adds a ten in her head. 48 + 10 = 58. Then 10 more: 68. Only the tens digit changes. No paper needed.
Do the same with hundreds. 325 + 100 = 425. 325 − 100 = 225. Only the hundreds digit moves. Try 640 − 200. Two hundreds down: 540, 440. So 640 − 200 = 440.
Break bigger jumps into tens. 57 + 30 is three tens more. 67, 77, 87. So 57 + 30 = 87. And 92 − 40 is four tens back. 82, 72, 62, 52. So 92 − 40 = 52.

words.d: doing math in your head without writing it down

look.title: Ten More Each Day
look.cite: Example: cups sold, going up by 10 each day
look.prompt: If the pattern keeps going, how many cups on Friday? What about Saturday?

check.why: Two tens more: 86, then 96. So 76 + 20 = 96.
One hundred less. The 4 becomes 3. So 383.
Three hundreds more: 350, 450, 550. So 250 + 300 = 550.

lessons.title: Why the Strategy Works
lessons.mainIdea: A good strategy works because it keeps the tens and ones in their places.
reading: Kai adds 48 + 36 by jumping. 48 + 30 = 78. Then 78 + 6 = 84. Why does this *strategy* work? Because 36 is just 30 and 6. Adding 30 and then 6 is the same as adding 36.
Rosa uses a different way. She makes 48 into 50. She takes 2 from 36 to do it. 50 + 34 = 84. Same answer! Moving 2 from one number to the other does not change the total.
When you *explain* a strategy, say what you did to the tens and ones. Say why the total did not change. Then check with a different way. If both ways match, you can trust the answer.

words.d: a plan or way to solve a problem
to tell how you did something and why it works

look.title: Two Ways to 73
look.text: Two students add 29 + 44. Mia jumps: 29 + 40 = 69, then 69 + 4 = 73. Leo makes a ten: he moves 1 from 44 to 29. That gives 30 + 43 = 73. Both get 73. Look closely at Leo's move.
look.prompt: Why does moving 1 from 44 to 29 keep the total the same?

check.q: Rosa solves 57 + 25 as 60 + 22. Why does this work?
choices: she moved 3 from 25 to 57, so the total stays 82
she took 3 away and lost them
check.why: 57 + 3 = 60 and 25 − 3 = 22. The total is still 82.

check.q: Kai adds 64 + 23 by jumping the tens first. What is his first jump?
check.why: Jump the tens first: 64 + 20 = 84. Then 84 + 3 = 87.

check.q: Kai gets 84 one way and 74 another way. What should he do?
check.why: Two different answers means one has a mistake. Check each step of both ways again.

review.why: 7 + 8 = 15. Trade ten ones for a ten. 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 tens. So 85.
Trade: 6 tens and 10 ones. 10 − 6 = 4. 6 − 2 = 4 tens. So 44.
One hundred more. The 5 becomes 6. So 616.
